glossary.definition: A document the MCP gateway publishes (RFC 9728) that names its authorization server and the scopes it understands. The first 401 points at it, so a client can find out how to get a token with no prior arrangement.
A document (RFC 8414) listing the identity provider's endpoints, supported grants, PKCE methods and client authentication methods, so the client needs no hard-coded configuration.

The client identifies itself by publishing a client document at a URL and using that URL as its client id. The identity provider fetches it to learn the redirect URI and the public keys, then checks them against its client acceptance policy.
A stored, versioned record that this member allowed this client to use this scope on this resource. Consent is necessary where required but never overrides policy.

The client authenticates to the token endpoint with a short signed assertion made with a key only it holds; the identity provider checks it against the published JWKS. It is client authentication, not sender constraint: a token already issued is still a bearer.

At sign-in the identity provider sends PingOne Protect the device and behaviour signals collected in the member's browser and gets back a risk level (low, medium or high), which it can use to step up the member or refuse to issue a code. Optionally Protect's bot detection can name the AI agent type; that claim is UNVERIFIED here. In this mock the evaluation is a stub with fixed values.
A one-time secret the client creates before the browser leg and proves at the token exchange, so a stolen authorization code is useless.
The access token names one audience (the MCP resource) and one scope, and lives minutes. The gateway rejects it anywhere else.
The service the gateway asks, with member, client, tool, action, resource and context, for Permit or Deny. The gateway enforces; the decision point decides.

sources.use: The metadata the first 401 points at.

sources.use: The sign-in configuration the client discovers.

cards.label: Step 1: Protected tool request
cards.description: The member asks the assistant for their benefits. The assistant calls the tool with no token and the gateway answers 401 with a pointer to its metadata.

cards.label: Step 2: Discover the resource
cards.description: The assistant reads the protected-resource metadata: which authorization server to trust and which scope this tool needs. Nobody at Northwind Health is involved.

cards.label: Step 3: Discover the OAuth configuration
cards.description: The authorization-server metadata says how to sign in: endpoints, PKCE, and that the client proves itself with a signed assertion.

cards.label: Step 4: Browser authorization
cards.description: The assistant sends the member to the identity provider. The browser makes the authorization request, so the assistant never sees the member credentials.

cards.label: Step 5: Client metadata lookup (CIMD)
cards.description: The client id is a URL. The identity provider fetches that document to learn the redirect URI and the keys, and checks them against its client acceptance policy.

cards.label: Step 6: Sign-in, risk evaluation and consent
cards.description: The member signs in and sees a consent prompt that names the assistant, the data and the purpose. While they do, the browser collects device and behaviour signals and the identity provider asks PingOne Protect for a risk level (a stub here); a high level can stop the code. Protect can optionally name the AI agent type (UNVERIFIED). Approve stores a consent record; Deny issues no code.

cards.label: Step 7: Code exchange and client verification
cards.description: The assistant trades the code for a token and proves who it is with a signed assertion. The identity provider checks the signature against the published keys.

cards.label: Step 8: Access token
cards.description: The token is bound to one audience and one scope, and lives minutes. The assistant holds it; it is not a session.

cards.label: Step 9: Gateway validation
cards.description: Every call carries the token. The gateway checks signature, issuer, audience, expiry, scope, member and consent before anything else happens.

cards.label: Step 10: Fine-grained decision
cards.description: The gateway asks the policy decision point whether this member, through this client, may do this action on this resource. A Deny stops the call here.

cards.label: Step 11: Downstream call
cards.description: Only after a Permit does the gateway call the benefits API, which returns only this member's data.

cards.label: Step 12: Authorized result
cards.description: The result goes back to the assistant, which explains it to the member. The assistant held its own signing key and a short-lived token, never the member's credentials.

cards.label: The assistant is never trusted
cards.description: The assistant only ever holds a token that lives for minutes; the gateway and the policy engine decide every call.

cards.label: Doctor and health
cards.description: Preflight checks and the demo-health/1 endpoint.
